title: Aurora Search Labs - POC check-in (Optimize cost savings + quality gates)
summary: Aurora shared early POC results (batching + KV cache changes) showing ~18–24% cost reduction on their top search assistant route with comparable latency. Redwood walked through how Optimize quality gates will be enforced before one-click/auto-apply: fast smoke gates (8–12 min) + full gates (35–60 min depending on prompt-set size), expected pass rates by change type, and how failures are handled (blocked apply, artifact links, reruns, quarantine for flaky suites, time-bound override policy). The group aligned on expanding gating to 2 additional routes, agreeing on baseline selection and prompt-set coverage, and setting operational expectations (gate execution latency SLO, paging thresholds, and escalation).
topics: POC cost savings so far and what changes drove it (batching/caching/quant profile)
Quality gate tiers: smoke vs full, runtime/cost bounds, pass-rate expectations
How failures are handled: block apply, rerun policy, override workflow, audit trail
Canary rollout coupling: promotion blocked on failed gates, auto-rollback hooks
Next-step plan to expand from one route to three routes + finalize success criteria
next_steps: Redwood to enable quality-gated Optimize recommendations for two additional Aurora routes (staging first, then limited prod).
Aurora to provide 200–300 representative prompts per route (including long-context and multilingual cases) and confirm allowed data retention for eval artifacts.
Redwood to share Console screenshots / access details for gate run artifacts + dashboard views and clarify who at Aurora should have override-request visibility.
Schedule a 30-min working session to pick baseline configs for quantization comparisons per GPU SKU and define acceptable regression thresholds for the search relevance rubric.
action_items: Yara Haddad - Send Aurora the route onboarding checklist for gating (prompt-set format, headers, redaction guidance) by 2026-02-24
Diego Ramos - Share recommended online canary signals (CTR proxy, refusal rate, empty answer rate, latency p95) + suggested alert thresholds by 2026-02-25
Dylan Brooks - Confirm Console UI fields Aurora will see for gate results (pass/fail reasons, artifact links, rerun button, override request) and provide sample screenshots by 2026-02-26
Ravi Singh (Aurora) - Export representative prompt set for Route B + Route C, include at least 30 long-context cases (>16k tokens) by 2026-02-27
Maya Chen (Aurora) - Confirm who can approve time-bound overrides on Aurora side and whether procurement needs audit-log export/SIEM support for the POC by 2026-02-28
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-20
Start time: 4:00 PM PT
Duration: 46 minutes
Call type: POC check-in

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Aditya Rao, Yara Haddad, Diego Ramos, Dylan Brooks
Aurora Search Labs: Maya Chen, Ravi Singh, Lena Koval (Tom Becker joined later)

Auto-summary (Fireflies)
- Discussed current savings and what Optimize changes were tested
- Reviewed quality gate pass/fail behavior, reruns, and overrides
- Agreed next steps to expand to more routes and finalize success criteria

Transcript
[00:00] Aditya Rao: Cool. Hey everyone. Thanks for making the time. Goal today is quick POC check-in: cost savings you’re seeing, how the quality gates behave in practice, and then what it takes to expand from the one route to a couple more.

[00:16] Maya Chen: Sounds good.

[00:18] Yara Haddad: Hi all.

[00:19] Diego Ramos: Hey.

[00:21] Dylan Brooks: Hi.

[00:26] Aditya Rao: Maya, do you want to start with where you’re at? Last time we were mostly on batching + some cache settings.

[00:35] Maya Chen: Yeah. So we ran the last two weeks mostly on the “search assistant” route, the one that does the answer synthesis after retrieval. The biggest win was batching. We saw, depending on time of day, like 18% to 24% lower cost per 1k tokens. Latency didn’t get worse, maybe slightly better because… I guess you guys were doing continuous batching.

[00:58] Ravi Singh: And for clarity, that was with the KV cache prefix thing turned on for the system prompt, right? Not the full prompt.

[01:06] Yara Haddad: Yeah, exactly. Prefix caching for the stable preamble + tool schema. Not caching user content.

[01:12] Lena Koval: One thing: we did see a couple spikes where p95 jumped. Not huge. Like from 680ms to 820ms for a window. I don’t know if that’s just load.

[01:26] Diego Ramos: That lines up with what we see when the batcher gets overly “ambitious” under burst and then backs off. We can tune the max wait. But that’s separate from quality gating, just to separate the concerns.

[01:40] Aditya Rao: Great. And on quality, did you notice any output differences? Like refusal weirdness or answer format drift.

[01:48] Maya Chen: Not from our spot checks. But we didn’t do systematic evals yet. Which is why we’re here.

[01:54] Aditya Rao: Totally. So let me frame the new behavior: any Optimize recommendation that changes batching policy, KV/prefix cache, or quant profile will trigger a gate run. If it doesn’t pass, apply is blocked. That includes one-click apply and also auto-apply.

[02:12] Ravi Singh: When you say “gate run”, that’s offline evaluation? Like running our prompts through old config and new config.

[02:19] Yara Haddad: Yep. Baseline vs candidate. Same model version pinned. The config diff is the only change. We compute deltas per metric, and then apply thresholds.

[02:29] Dylan Brooks: And in Console, you’ll see “Pending / Running / Passed / Failed / Overridden” with an artifact link. Artifact is basically the eval report: per prompt, output snippets, rubric scores, and the diff summary.

[02:44] Maya Chen: What’s the runtime? Like how long does it block us.

[02:48] Aditya Rao: Two tiers. Fast smoke gates: usually 8 to 12 minutes. Full gates: 35 to 60 minutes depending on prompt set size and region capacity.

[03:00] Ravi Singh: That’s per recommendation. So if we have like three recommendations, it’s three eval runs.

[03:06] Yara Haddad: Correct. Although we try to coalesce if the diffs are compatible. But in MVP assume one per change set.

[03:14] Lena Koval: And the cost of the eval itself is on us?

[03:17] Aditya Rao: During POC, we’re covering it. In GA it’s billed like usage but we’re keeping it bounded; also we don’t run full gates for every minor tweak if policy says smoke gate is sufficient.

[03:29] Maya Chen: How often do they fail? Like what’s normal.

[03:33] Aditya Rao: It depends on config type. Batching and caching changes typically pass at a pretty high rate, say 80%+ once tuned. Quantization profile switches are riskier; internal beta we’re seeing more like 55% to 70% pass depending on model family and prompt mix.

[03:52] Ravi Singh: Okay. That makes sense. Quant can shift outputs.

[03:55] Diego Ramos: And we’ve got flake handling too. Like if the eval is noisy—rubric variance, intermittent tool calls—then it will automatically rerun once. If it’s still unstable, it gets marked “flaky” and the suite can be quarantined so it doesn’t page the world.

[04:13] Lena Koval: Wait, “quarantined” meaning it doesn’t block apply?

[04:17] Diego Ramos: No, sorry, quarantine means that prompt set is flagged as unreliable and removed from gating until it’s fixed. We don’t silently allow apply; it becomes a policy decision. Usually we’d replace it with a stable subset.

[04:32] Dylan Brooks: In the UI you’ll see “Failure reason: regression” versus “Failure reason: flake / insufficient confidence.” They’re different states.

[04:40] Maya Chen: And in a fail case, what do we do? Just… can’t take the savings.

[04:46] Aditya Rao: Default is you can’t apply to production traffic. You can either (a) accept, don’t apply, (b) adjust the config recommendation—less aggressive batching, different cache scope—rerun, or (c) request an override.

[04:59] Ravi Singh: Override is like admin bypass.

[05:02] Aditya Rao: It is, but time-bound and audited. It requires an approver role, reason, and expiration. We’re tightening who can do it because of a near-miss internally.

[05:14] Maya Chen: What’s the expiration like? Days? Hours?

[05:17] Dylan Brooks: Default we’ve been doing 24 hours for “keep the lights on” situations, and up to 7 days for planned exceptions, but only if there’s a follow-up ticket linked. That’s policy-driven.

[05:30] Lena Koval: If we override and then it causes an issue online, does it auto rollback?

[05:35] Diego Ramos: If you’re using the rollout controller with canary, yes. We can wire “gate failed” to block promotion, and separately we can use online signals to trigger rollback. Those are two different safety nets.

[05:48] Ravi Singh: Let’s talk about canary. Today our rollout is: we flip config on one environment, then gradually move traffic. Where does gating plug in.

[05:58] Aditya Rao: Before canary starts, you need a passed gate run (or an override). During canary, if gates are later invalidated—like you change the diff again—it’ll stop promotion. It won’t automatically change your config unless you allow auto-rollback.

[06:14] Maya Chen: So it’s defense in depth.

[06:16] Aditya Rao: Exactly.

[06:19] Yara Haddad: And for your POC we can keep it simple: we’ll gate the next recommendation, then run canary on 5% traffic for 30 minutes, look at the online signals Diego mentioned.

[06:32] Ravi Singh: What are the offline metrics? Like what’s a “pass.”

[06:36] Yara Haddad: For your use case we’ve been mapping to a couple things: (1) task success rate, which is basically “did it answer using retrieved context and not hallucinate,” (2) rubric score for relevance and completeness, and (3) format adherence—like JSON/tool schema when you use tool calling.

[06:55] Maya Chen: Is there a numeric threshold? Like “no more than X drop.”

[06:59] Yara Haddad: Yep. Example: rubric mean cannot drop more than 0.5 points on a 10-point rubric, and task success cannot drop more than 1.0 percentage point, with a confidence requirement. Those numbers can be tuned. We also require minimum sample sizes so a tiny set doesn’t pass on noise.

[07:18] Ravi Singh: If we give you 200 prompts, is that enough.

[07:21] Yara Haddad: For smoke, yes. For full gates, we’d like 500+ eventually, but we can start with 200–300 and then expand. Also we want coverage of your “hard cases”: long context, multilingual, adversarial queries.

[07:37] Lena Koval: We do have long contexts. Like 20k tokens sometimes.

[07:41] Diego Ramos: That’s exactly where some quant profiles get weird. We’ve seen regressions only on long-context prompts. So we should explicitly tag those and make sure they’re in the gate suite.

[07:53] Maya Chen: The thing procurement is going to ask me is: what’s the operational burden? Like do we need a person watching gates.

[08:00] Aditya Rao: In steady state, no. It’s designed so “safe by default” is the path. If gates fail a lot, that’s a signal either the recommendation is too aggressive or the prompt set is too brittle.

[08:12] Dylan Brooks: And you’ll have a dashboard: gate funnel (suggested → gated → passed → applied), failures by config type, and flake rate.

[08:21] Ravi Singh: What’s a normal flake rate.

[08:23] Diego Ramos: We’re targeting under 5% of runs requiring rerun, and under 2% ending in “inconclusive / flaky” after rerun. If it’s higher we treat it as an incident on our side because it blocks teams.

[08:38] Lena Koval: Good. Because we had a bad experience with an internal eval suite just being flaky all the time.

[08:45] Aditya Rao: Same. That’s why we’re building quarantine tooling.

[08:51] Maya Chen: How does this relate to the cost savings number? Like if you add 60 minutes of eval time, it kind of offsets.

[08:58] Aditya Rao: Fair question. The gate run cost is one-time per change, while the savings are per-token ongoing. For a high-volume route like yours, even a 15% savings pays back quickly. But we’re still bounding gate cost and time, and that’s why we have smoke gates.

[09:14] Ravi Singh: If smoke passes but full fails, what happens.

[09:18] Yara Haddad: Then you’re blocked at the point where policy requires full. Some customers will have policy “smoke only for batching, full for quant.” That’s configurable per route and tier.

[09:30] Maya Chen: For us: I’m okay with smoke-only for batching and cache. For quant, we should be stricter.

[09:36] Aditya Rao: That’s what we usually recommend.

[09:39] Dylan Brooks: We can set a gating policy per route. So Route A maybe smoke for batching/cache; Route A quant requires full gate. For Route B you can do full across the board if you want.

[09:53] Lena Koval: Route B is lower volume but more “high stakes.” It’s the customer support triage assistant.

[10:00] Maya Chen: Exactly.

[10:02] Diego Ramos: For that one we should also include “escalation suggestion correctness.” Like it shouldn’t tell users to do something unsafe.

[10:10] Ravi Singh: We have a small set of “do not do this” prompts.

[10:14] Yara Haddad: Great, those become hard-gate prompts.

[10:18] Aditya Rao: Okay, so expansion. Today we’re gating on Route A only in staging, right?

[10:25] Lena Koval: Yes. We didn’t turn on prod gating because we weren’t sure it wouldn’t block stuff.

[10:30] Aditya Rao: Understood. Proposal: next week we enable gating on Route A in prod but only for Optimize applies—not for your manual config changes yet. Then we add Route B and Route C in staging first.

[10:46] Maya Chen: I like that.

[10:48] Ravi Singh: What about manual changes. We do sometimes tweak batch sizes ourselves.

[10:52] Aditya Rao: MVP is we log them and we try to gate where we can. But enforcement at the “apply boundary” is strongest when it goes through Optimize/Console. For manual, we’ll at least capture audit trail, and we can run a gate run optionally.

[11:10] Lena Koval: So no silent drift.

[11:12] Aditya Rao: Exactly.

[11:14] Dylan Brooks: And you’ll see those in the audit view: “manual change” versus “Optimize suggested,” with who did it.

[11:22] Maya Chen: Audit view helps.

[11:26] Ravi Singh: Can you talk about artifacts and data retention. Are you storing our prompts.

[11:32] Dylan Brooks: Artifacts are stored with retention settings. For the POC we’re doing 14 days by default. Prompts can be hashed/redacted if needed, but that reduces debugging. We can discuss what’s acceptable.

[11:46] Maya Chen: We need to check with legal. We can probably do 14 days if it’s encrypted and access-controlled.

[11:52] Aditya Rao: It is. Encryption at rest and RBAC. If you’re on hosted, artifacts are in our secured store; for private deployments later, artifacts can live in your bucket.

[12:06] Ravi Singh: Okay.

[12:09] Diego Ramos: Also, just to set expectations: gate execution latency can vary by region. If you run in EU-West and GPU capacity is tight, full gates can hit timeouts. We’ve been working on retries and region failover.

[12:23] Lena Koval: We did see a timeout once.

[12:25] Diego Ramos: Yeah. We’re tracking it. We’ve added a “gate runtime SLO” internally.

[12:31] Aditya Rao: For your POC, your traffic is US-West mostly, so we should be okay.

[12:37] Maya Chen: Great.

[12:39] Ravi Singh: Back to pass rates. If we see a failure, can we debug. Like is it obvious what changed.

[12:45] Yara Haddad: The report shows per-prompt deltas. Like “prompt 37: baseline answered with citations, candidate dropped a citation” or “format violation.” It’s not perfect but it’s actionable.

[12:58] Dylan Brooks: Plus links to the config diff: “batch_max_wait_ms changed from 8 to 20” etc.

[13:05] Lena Koval: Nice.

[13:08] Maya Chen: Okay. What do you need from us to expand.

[13:12] Yara Haddad: Two things: prompt sets for Route B and Route C, and a baseline config selection. For quant gating, baseline is per GPU SKU. If you’re on A100 vs H100, we pick the baseline accordingly.

[13:27] Ravi Singh: We’re on H100 for prod. Staging is mixed.

[13:30] Yara Haddad: Then baseline will be pinned to H100 for the full gate run to avoid mixing performance/behavior.

[13:38] Diego Ramos: For online canary, we’ll track refusal rate and “empty answer” rate, plus any custom quality signal you have. If you have click-through or resolution proxy, that’s gold.

[13:52] Maya Chen: We have a proxy: user edits the answer before sending.

[13:56] Diego Ramos: Great. That can be a canary guardrail.

[14:00] (crosstalk)

[14:01] Dylan Brooks: Sorry, quick note: some of those signals require you to send a header or event. We’ll send the instrumentation doc.

[14:09] Lena Koval: Okay.

[14:12] Aditya Rao: We’re at time-ish, but before we wrap—Tom from procurement was going to join. Is he on?

[14:19] Tom Becker: Hey, sorry, I’m here. I caught the last couple minutes.

[14:24] Aditya Rao: Hey Tom. Quick recap: we’re making sure Optimize cost-saving changes can’t ship without quality gates. It’s pass/fail evals with audit trail, plus canary integration.

[14:36] Tom Becker: My question is always: who can override, and can we export audit logs.

[14:41] Dylan Brooks: Override is restricted by RBAC, time-bound, and requires a reason. Every gate run and override emits an audit event. Export to SIEM is supported via our audit log export; we can share the format.

[14:55] Tom Becker: Good. And if it fails, it’s blocked, not “best effort.”

[14:59] Aditya Rao: Correct. Blocked by default.

[15:02] Tom Becker: Okay.

[15:04] Maya Chen: That’s what I needed.

[15:06] Aditya Rao: Great. So next steps: Ravi will send prompt sets for two routes, we’ll enable prod gating for Route A, and we’ll schedule a working session on thresholds and baselines.

[15:18] Ravi Singh: Yep.

[15:20] Lena Koval: Works.

[15:22] Diego Ramos: I’ll send canary signal suggestions.

[15:25] Dylan Brooks: I’ll send screenshots of the gate results UI and what you’ll see.

[15:30] Aditya Rao: Perfect. Thanks everyone.

[15:33] Meeting ended
